content: Iron(II) sulfide is a chemical compound with the molecular formula FeS. In practical applications, iron sulfides are often non-stoichiometric in nature. When in powdered form, iron sulfide is pyrophoric, meaning it can spontaneously ignite in air. The compound FeS can be synthesized through a direct reaction between elemental iron and sulfur. Iron sulfide exists in several distinct forms, each differing in stoichiometry and physical properties: Pyrrhotite (Fe₁₋ₓS): This is a mineral form of iron sulfide and also a byproduct of the Desulfovibrio bacteria. Pyrrhotite exhibits ferrimagnetic properties. Troilite (FeS): Structurally similar to pyrrhotite, troilite does not exhibit ferromagnetic properties. Mackinawite (Fe₁₊ₓS): This is the least stable form of iron sulfide and has a layered structural arrangement. Pyrite (FeS₂): Known as fool's gold due to its gold-like appearance, pyrite is a mineral form of iron disulfide. Iron sulfides are often used pedagogically to illustrate various chemical principles. For example: The synthesis of iron(II) sulfide from iron and sulfur is an exothermic reaction, releasing more energy than it absorbs. While elemental iron exhibits ferromagnetism, iron sulfides do not. When iron sulfide reacts with hydrochloric acid (HCl), the acidic properties of HCl and the release of pungent hydrogen sulfide gas can be demonstrated. In biological and biochemical contexts, ferrous sulfide (FeS) appears as a visible black precipitate in peptone iron agar, a growth medium used to differentiate microorganisms. This medium contains the amino acid cysteine and ferric citrate as a chemical indicator. Microorganisms that produce the enzyme cysteine desulfhydrase catalyze the release of hydrogen sulfide gas from cysteine. The hydrogen sulfide then reacts with ferric citrate to form ferrous sulfide, which serves as a diagnostic marker.
